title: Leg 62 — Chimney Rock and Scotts Bluff
subtitle: Chimney Rock, the North Platte Valley, Scotts Bluff and Alliance
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. We are leaving Kimball and heading northeast toward the North Platte Valley, where two of the great landmarks of the overland trails come into view. After waypoint one, Chimney Rock will be ahead and to the right. Farther west, Scotts Bluff will rise off the left side as we approach waypoint three. The final portion turns away from the North Platte toward the Wildcat Hills and the open country around Alliance. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: Leaving Kimball
blocks.text: We are leaving Kimball and heading northeast across the Nebraska Panhandle. The country below is still high, dry plains, but ahead the land begins to organize itself around the North Platte River, one of the great travel corridors of the nineteenth-century West.

blocks.title: Toward the Great Platte River Road
blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of emigrants followed the Platte and North Platte west toward Oregon, California and Utah. The broad river valley offered water, grass and a comparatively gentle route across the plains. Most travelers walked beside their wagons for much of the journey, saving the animals' strength and wagon space for supplies.

blocks.title: Landmarks begin to rise from the plains
blocks.text: The famous formations ahead are remnants of much larger layers of sediment that once covered this region. Over millions of years, the North Platte and its tributaries cut down through softer clay and sandstone, leaving isolated buttes, ridges and spires standing above the valley.

blocks.title: The skyline that told travelers they were west
blocks.text: For emigrants who had spent weeks crossing relatively open prairie, the first strange shapes along the North Platte carried enormous psychological weight. Features like Chimney Rock and Scotts Bluff were not just scenery; they were unmistakable confirmation that the landscape of the West was finally changing.

blocks.title: Chimney Rock ahead-right
blocks.text: Chimney Rock should now be ahead and to the right, about four miles away. The isolated spire rises more than three hundred feet from its base and is distinctive enough that nineteenth-century travelers could recognize it from many miles across the valley.

blocks.title: The most-written-about landmark on the trail
blocks.text: More emigrant diaries mentioned Chimney Rock than any other landmark on the Oregon Trail. To people who had never seen the geology of the American West, the narrow spire seemed almost impossible. Travelers sketched it, argued about its height and frequently camped nearby simply to get a closer look.

blocks.title: A landmark that keeps changing
blocks.text: The formation has changed noticeably since the wagon-train era. History Nebraska estimates the present spire at about one hundred twenty feet tall, with the tip about three hundred twenty-five feet above the base. Early travelers thought it might collapse within their lifetimes, but erosion has been slower than many of them expected.

blocks.title: Bayard and the irrigated valley
blocks.spokenLabel: Bayard and the North Platte Valley
blocks.text: Bayard is close by in the valley now. In the early twentieth century, large irrigation projects transformed this dry region into productive farmland. Sugar beets became especially important, and processing plants were built in several North Platte Valley towns as irrigated acreage expanded dramatically.

blocks.title: A man-made green corridor
blocks.text: The North Platte Valley below is far greener than the surrounding uplands because generations of canals and later federal reclamation projects moved river water across the fields. By the early twentieth century, irrigation had turned sagebrush and rangeland into crops such as alfalfa, beans, potatoes and sugar beets.

blocks.title: Scotts Bluff off the left
blocks.text: Scotts Bluff should now be prominent off the left side. The sandstone and clay bluffs rise roughly eight hundred feet above the North Platte River valley. From our route, the main mass is several miles away, but it is large enough to dominate this part of the skyline.

blocks.title: Mitchell Pass and the wagon bottleneck
blocks.text: Early wagon trains had to swing well south around the bluff through Robidoux Pass. Around 1850, Mitchell Pass was opened closer to the river, saving about eight miles. The new route was narrow enough that wagons often traveled single file, and the concentrated traffic carved a broad trail swale that can still be traced today.

blocks.title: The uncertain story behind the name
blocks.text: The bluff carries the name of Hiram Scott, a fur-trade employee who died in this region in 1828. The exact circumstances became tangled in frontier legend, with different versions describing illness, abandonment and a grim final journey. What is certain is that his name became permanently attached to one of the great landmarks of the western trails.

blocks.title: Gering and Scottsbluff beside the river
blocks.text: The communities of Gering and Scottsbluff lie close by on opposite sides of the North Platte. Gering was established first, while Scottsbluff developed rapidly around the turn of the twentieth century. Irrigation and the sugar-beet industry helped turn this valley into one of western Nebraska's major agricultural centers.

blocks.title: Wildcat Hills behind-left
blocks.text: As we turn northeast, the rugged Wildcat Hills are falling behind and to the left. These pine- and juniper-studded escarpments are a sharp contrast to the open prairie and irrigated valley we have just crossed.

blocks.title: Unexpected wildlife in the Nebraska Panhandle
blocks.text: The Wildcat Hills support a surprisingly varied mix of wildlife. Nebraska Game and Parks lists bighorn sheep, mule deer, wild turkey, bobcats and coyotes here, and even occasional moose. The rough canyons also hold mountain mahogany, a shrub uncommon elsewhere in Nebraska.

blocks.title: Leaving the North Platte corridor
blocks.spokenLabel: the high plains north of the river
blocks.text: The North Platte Valley is dropping away behind us now. Ahead, the terrain becomes broader and drier again as we move toward the western edge of Nebraska's Sandhills and the railroad town of Alliance.

blocks.title: Toward the Sandhills
blocks.text: This open country approaches the western edge of the Nebraska Sandhills, one of the largest grass-stabilized dune regions in the world. The dunes are old enough and well-vegetated enough that from the air they can look like rolling natural hills rather than piles of sand.

blocks.title: Homesteading on much larger claims
blocks.text: Ordinary 160-acre homesteads often proved too small for this dry grazing country. The Kincaid Act of 1904 allowed settlers in parts of western Nebraska to claim as much as 640 acres, helping spread ranch settlement across land where farming on eastern scales made little sense.

blocks.title: Alliance grows around the railroad
blocks.text: Alliance began in the late 1880s with the Burlington and Missouri River Railroad. The railroad set aside land for tracks, shops and a roundhouse, and the town grew quickly as a shipping and service center for ranchers and homesteaders. It later became one of the important railroad towns of the Nebraska Panhandle.

blocks.title: The courthouse that came to town by rail
blocks.text: Alliance won the Box Butte County seat after a bitter series of elections, but there was still the problem of the courthouse sitting about twenty miles away in Hemingford. In 1899, crews placed the entire building on railroad cars and moved it to Alliance, a feat dramatic enough to attract national magazine coverage.

blocks.title: Alliance off the left
blocks.text: Alliance is coming into view off the left side. The airport sits southeast of town, so we will reach the field without flying directly over downtown. The city's railroad roots are still visible in the large rail facilities that remain an important part of the local economy.

blocks.title: Carhenge farther left
blocks.text: Farther off the left side is one of Nebraska's strangest attractions: Carhenge. It is a small target from the airplane, so it may be difficult to identify. Artist Jim Reinders and about thirty-five relatives built the Stonehenge replica in 1987 using thirty-nine automobiles, all painted gray. The project began as a memorial to Reinders' father and was dedicated on the summer solstice.

blocks.title: A World War Two training field
blocks.text: The airport ahead carries a major World War Two story. Alliance Army Air Base trained more than fourteen thousand paratroopers and glider pilots for wartime operations. After the war, the military field became the municipal airport we are approaching now.

blocks.title: Alliance Municipal Airport
blocks.text: Alliance Municipal Airport is just ahead. This leg has crossed a remarkable slice of western Nebraska, from the most famous landmarks of the wagon trails to irrigated farm country, rugged bluffs, Sandhills ranchland and a railroad-and-aviation town on the plains.
